items.stem: ‘The Treaty of Versailles was too harsh on Germany.’ Discuss.
items.answer: For: Germany lost about 13 per cent of its European territory and all colonies. Reparations and the war guilt clause caused deep resentment. Germany was not allowed to negotiate. Against: Germany remained united and potentially the strongest power in Europe. Germany had imposed harsher terms on Russia at Brest-Litovsk. Reparations were within Germany's capacity, and much was never paid. Judgement: the treaty was harsh enough to cause lasting resentment but not harsh enough to prevent German recovery, which was its main weakness.

items.stem: In 1919 J. M. Keynes published The Economic Consequences of the Peace. How far did the peace settlement of 1919-20 achieve the aims of the peacemakers?
items.answer: For: France gained Alsace-Lorraine and a demilitarised Rhineland. The League of Nations was created. Britain gained colonies and the German fleet was removed. Against: Clemenceau did not get the Rhine frontier or an Anglo-American guarantee. Wilson's League was rejected by the US Senate. Self-determination was applied inconsistently. Judgement: each peacemaker gained some aims, but the settlement satisfied none of them fully and left Germany resentful.

items.answer: For: The USA was the world's greatest economic power, so sanctions were less effective. Britain and France were left to lead and lacked the resources and will. items.stem: ‘The League of Nations was weakened from the start by the absence of the USA.’ How far do you agree?
items.answer: For: The USA was the world's greatest economic power, so sanctions were less effective. Britain and France were left to lead and lacked the resources and will. The League looked like a club of the victors. Against: The structure of unanimity and lack of an army were greater weaknesses. The absence of Germany and the USSR also weakened it. Britain and France put national interests first. The League had successes in the 1920s without the USA. Judgement: the absence of the USA was a serious weakness, but the League's structure and the attitudes of Britain and France were more fundamental.

items.stem: In 1923 Mussolini occupied the Greek island of Corfu. Explain why the League failed to resolve the Corfu and Vilna disputes.
items.answer: Italy was a great power and a permanent member of the Council. Britain and France put their own interests first. The Conference of Ambassadors overrode the League. items.stem: A revision guide lists these reasons why disarmament made little progress in the 1920s. A: The Geneva Protocol of 1924 was rejected by Britain. B: Powers disagreed over what counted as armaments. C: France feared Germany and would not disarm without security guarantees. Explain which of these was the most important reason.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: The Geneva Protocol of 1924 was rejected by Britain. B: Powers disagreed over what counted as armaments. C: France feared Germany and would not disarm without security guarantees. Possible judgement: disarmament failed because France would not reduce its forces without security guarantees that Britain would not give.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: ‘The Locarno Treaties brought real security to Europe.’ How far do you agree with this view?
items.answer: For: Germany accepted its western borders voluntarily. They led to German entry to the League in 1926. They created a spirit of cooperation. Against: They left Germany's eastern borders open to revision. They depended on Stresemann and economic prosperity. They were made outside the League, weakening it. The spirit of Locarno collapsed with the Depression. Judgement: Locarno improved relations, but it rested on prosperity and goodwill and left the eastern question unresolved, so security was more apparent than real.

items.stem: Which of these statements is accurate?

items.stem: Aisha is planning an answer to the question: “How far did the peace settlement of 1919-20 achieve the aims of the peacemakers?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Aisha could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: each peacemaker gained some aims, but the settlement satisfied none of them fully and left Germany resentful. Support: France gained Alsace-Lorraine and a demilitarised Rhineland. The League of Nations was created. Challenge: Clemenceau did not get the Rhine frontier or an Anglo-American guarantee. Wilson's League was rejected by the US Senate.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Study Source A. Source A: J. M. Keynes, The Economic Consequences of the Peace, 1919 (summary). Keynes argued that reparations were far beyond Germany's capacity to pay and would ruin the economy of Europe. Assess the reliability of Source A as evidence about the economic terms.
items.answer: Reliable because Keynes was a Treasury adviser at the conference. Less reliable because he had resigned in protest and wanted to change policy. Cross-reference: It does not consider French security needs. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view, but it needs to be tested against other evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point about the content; up to 2 marks for using the provenance (author, date, purpose, audience) to judge reliability; up to 2 marks for cross-referencing with own knowledge; 1 mark for a supported overall judgement [6]

items.stem: Study Sources B and D. Source B: a German newspaper, Deutsche Zeitung, 28 June 1919 (translated, abridged). “Vengeance! German nation! Today in the Hall of Mirrors the disgraceful treaty is being signed. Do not forget it.” Source D: a historian writing in 1990 (illustrative). “Germany was defeated but not destroyed. It kept its industry and its unity; the treaty was too severe to conciliate and too lenient to restrain.” Identify one similarity and one difference between Sources B and D on the peace settlement of 1919-20.
items.answer: Source B: It shows German anger and a desire for revenge. Source D: The historian argues that the treaty was not too harsh in itself but failed to weaken Germany permanently. A similarity and a difference must each be supported by details from both sources.

items.stem: What is meant by “collective security”?
options: The idea that members would act together against an aggressor.
A former German or Ottoman territory governed by a victorious power on behalf of the League.
The League body that supervised the government of mandated territories.
Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles, which made Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage caused by the war.

items.stem: The Covenant of the League of Nations formed the first part of the Treaty of Versailles. How far was the League of Nations designed to fail?
items.answer: For: Unanimity rule made decisions slow. No army to enforce decisions. Membership excluded key powers. Against: Its agencies achieved real success in health, refugees and labour. Judgement: the League had serious design flaws but was not designed to fail; it worked when the great powers supported it.

items.stem: How far did the international agreements of the 1920s reduce the risk of war?
items.answer: For: The Washington Conference prevented a naval race in the Pacific. Locarno and Germany's entry to the League eased Franco-German tension. The Dawes and Young Plans eased reparations disputes. Against: Kellogg-Briand had no means of enforcement. Disarmament failed. Agreements depended on US loans and collapsed in the Depression. Judgement: they reduced tension while prosperity lasted, but had no means of enforcement and did not survive the Depression.
